## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land since my early twenties. Here in Quzhou, everyone grows winter wheat followed by summer maize — that's the rotation. The soil is flat, the extension station tells us to do it, my father did it, and it makes sense because the land doesn't rest idle. Two crops a year.

I have about 10 mu of contracted land. After the summer maize comes off in late September, I'll rotary-till and plant wheat around October 10th. I'll buy improved seed — Jimai 22 or whatever the village supply cooperative is stocking this year — not the old varieties, those yield too low. I'll put down compound fertilizer as base and then top-dress urea at jointing. Four irrigations for wheat: bottom water before planting, one in winter so it doesn't freeze out, one at jointing, one at heading. I'll spray herbicide in winter and hit aphids and powdery mildew in April.

After wheat harvest in June, I go straight into maize — no-till, direct seeding, hybrid seed like Zhengdan 958. Summer rains usually handle most of the water. I'll do one irrigation if July turns dry. Top-dress urea at the big bell stage. One pass for corn borer, maybe another for fall armyworm since that's been spreading.

I don't grow vegetables or anything else — too much trouble, no good market connection, and I sometimes help my brother-in-law with his land in busy seasons, so keeping it simple works for me.

I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed purchased from the village cooperative because yields are reliably higher than traditional varieties. Wheat gets four irrigations — a necessity given the semi-arid climate — while summer maize relies mainly on monsoon rainfall with one supplemental irrigation as insurance. Fertilizer rates follow what the local extension station recommends and what my neighbors use. Tillage is rotary before wheat to work in maize stubble, then no-till direct seeding for maize to save time and cost after the wheat harvest window is short.
